lesson.title: Four Dead in Ohio
lesson.summary: On May 4, 1970, Ohio National Guard troops opened fire on unarmed student protesters at Kent State University during demonstrations against the US invasion of Cambodia, killing four students and wounding nine others in a moment that shocked the nation and deepened its divisions over the war.
lesson.body:
On April 30, 1970, President Nixon announced in a televised address that US and South Vietnamese forces were invading neighboring Cambodia to strike at North Vietnamese and Viet Cong sanctuaries there. For an anti-war movement that had believed Nixon was winding the war down, the news that he was instead expanding it into a new country felt like a betrayal, and it triggered protests on college campuses across the country within days.

At Kent State University in Ohio, demonstrations included the burning of the campus ROTC building, and Ohio Governor James Rhodes ordered the National Guard onto campus to restore order, calling the protesters part of a threat to the state. Tensions between guardsmen and students remained high over the following days. On May 4, 1970, during a rally that guard commanders had declared illegal, guardsmen advanced on and then retreated from a crowd of students, some of whom threw rocks and taunted them, before a group of guardsmen turned and fired into the crowd, discharging dozens of rounds in about thirteen seconds.

Four students, Allison Krause, Jeffrey Miller, Sandra Scheuer, and William Schroeder, were killed, and nine others were wounded. Some of the victims had been actively protesting; others were simply walking to class or observing from a distance. No guardsman was ever convicted in connection with the deaths. Just ten days later, on May 14 and 15, 1970, police and state highway patrol officers in Mississippi fired on students at Jackson State College, killing two Black students, an episode that received far less national attention, a disparity that reflected the racial inequities running through American life at the time.

The shootings at Kent State set off a wave of national outrage and grief, prompting a student strike that closed hundreds of college campuses and inspiring a well known protest song recorded that year by Crosby, Stills, Nash and Young. For many Americans, the sight of National Guard troops killing college students on American soil made vivid, in a way overseas battlefield reports could not, just how deeply the war had come to divide the country against itself. That shock helped fuel the distrust of government secrecy and official justification for the war that would soon explode into full view with the release of the Pentagon Papers.
